recipes.title: Parker House Rolls
recipes.description: The iconic folded dinner roll created at Boston's Parker House Hotel—tender, buttery, and perfect.
instructions: Dissolve yeast in warm milk (110°F). Let stand 5 minutes until foamy.
Add sugar, melted butter, salt, and egg. Mix well.
Gradually add flour to form a soft dough.
Knead until smooth and elastic, about 8 minutes.
Place in a greased bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled.
Punch down. Roll dough to 1/2-inch thickness.
Cut with a 2.5-inch round cutter. Brush each round with melted butter.
Fold in half, pressing edges lightly. Place on greased baking sheets.
Cover and let rise 30 minutes.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15-18 minutes until golden.
Brush hot rolls with more butter.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Created at Boston's Parker House Hotel around 1870, these rolls became a standard in Fannie Farmer's groundbreaking cookbook. The signature fold creates layers of buttery tenderness.

recipes.title: Boston Baked Beans
recipes.description: The definitive New England baked beans, slow-cooked with molasses and salt pork.
instructions: Soak beans overnight. Drain, cover with fresh water, and simmer until skins crack when blown upon, about 45 minutes.
Preheat oven to 300°F (150°C).
Place whole onion in bottom of bean pot. Add drained beans.
Mix molasses, brown sugar, mustard, salt, pepper, and boiling water. Pour over beans.
Score salt pork and press into top of beans.
Cover and bake 6-8 hours, adding water as needed to keep beans covered.
Uncover for last hour to brown the pork.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Fannie Farmer's baked beans recipe codified what Boston housewives had made for generations. The slow baking transforms humble beans into something transcendent.

recipes.title: Fannie Farmer Sugar Cookies
recipes.description: The original standardized sugar cookie recipe, perfect for rolling and cutting.
instructions: Beat butter and sugar until light and fluffy.
Add eggs and vanilla; beat well.
Whisk flour, baking powder, and salt. Add to butter mixture.
Divide dough in half. Wrap in plastic and refrigerate 1 hour.
Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Line baking sheets with parchment.
Roll dough to 1/4-inch thickness on floured surface.
Cut with cookie cutters. Place on prepared sheets.
Bake 8-10 minutes until edges are barely golden.
Cool on pan 2 minutes, then transfer to rack.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Before Fannie Farmer, recipes called for 'a lump of butter the size of an egg.' Her standardized measurements made this cookie recipe—and countless others—reproducible.

recipes.title: Indian Pudding
recipes.description: A colonial-era cornmeal and molasses pudding, baked slowly until custardy.
instructions: Preheat oven to 300°F (150°C). Butter a 2-quart baking dish.
Scald 3 cups milk in a saucepan.
Slowly whisk in cornmeal. Cook, stirring, until thickened, about 5 minutes.
Remove from heat. Add molasses, sugar, butter, salt, ginger, and cinnamon.
Beat eggs with remaining 1 cup cold milk. Stir into cornmeal mixture.
Pour into prepared dish.
Bake 2-3 hours until set but still slightly jiggly.
Serve warm with vanilla ice cream.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: This pudding dates to colonial times when cornmeal was called 'Indian meal.' The long, slow bake creates a custardy texture with a caramelized top.

recipes.title: Boston Brown Bread
recipes.description: Traditional steamed bread made with rye, cornmeal, and molasses—essential with baked beans.
instructions: Grease two 1-pound coffee cans or a 2-quart pudding mold.
Whisk rye flour, cornmeal, whole wheat flour, baking soda, and salt.
Add buttermilk and molasses. Stir until combined. Fold in raisins if using.
Fill molds 2/3 full. Cover tightly with foil.
Place on a rack in a large pot. Add boiling water to come halfway up molds.
Cover pot and steam 2.5-3 hours, adding water as needed.
Remove from molds. Slice while warm with a string or serrated knife.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: This steamed bread has been a New England tradition since colonial times. The three flours create a dense, moist texture that's perfect spread with cream cheese or butter.

recipes.title: Old-Fashioned Gingerbread
recipes.description: Moist, warmly spiced gingerbread that fills the kitchen with its aroma.
instructions: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a 9x13 inch pan.
Beat butter and sugar until fluffy. Add egg and molasses; beat well.
Whisk flour, baking soda, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and salt.
Add flour mixture alternately with hot water, beginning and ending with flour.
Pour into prepared pan.
Bake 35-40 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
Serve warm with whipped cream.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Gingerbread has been an American favorite since colonial times. This soft, cake-style version was a staple of New England baking, perfect with afternoon tea or as dessert.

recipes.title: Fannie Farmer Popovers
recipes.description: Dramatically puffed, hollow rolls with crispy exteriors and tender interiors.
instructions: Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C). Generously grease a popover pan or 6-cup muffin tin.
Beat eggs. Add milk, flour, salt, and melted butter. Beat until smooth.
Fill each cup about 2/3 full.
Bake at 450°F for 20 minutes.
Reduce temperature to 350°F (175°C) without opening oven. Bake 15-20 minutes more until deeply golden.
Pierce each popover with a knife to release steam.
Serve immediately with butter.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Fannie Farmer's popover recipe was precise: the high initial heat creates steam, making them 'pop' dramatically over the pan. The key is never opening the oven until they're done.

recipes.title: Boston Cream Pie
recipes.description: Fannie Farmer's legendary cake: two layers of sponge with pastry cream, topped with chocolate glaze.
instructions: For cake: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease two 9-inch round pans.
Whisk flour, baking powder, and salt. Beat butter and sugar until fluffy. Add eggs and vanilla.
Add flour mixture alternately with milk. Divide between pans.
Bake 25-30 minutes. Cool completely.
For filling: Whisk yolks, sugar, and cornstarch. Heat milk until simmering.
Slowly whisk hot milk into yolks. Return to pot and cook, stirring, until thick.
Remove from heat, add vanilla. Cover and chill.
For glaze: Melt chocolate with butter and corn syrup. Cool slightly.
Place one cake layer on plate. Spread with pastry cream. Top with second layer.
Pour chocolate glaze over top, letting it drip down sides.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Despite its name, this is actually a cake—created at Boston's Parker House Hotel in the 1850s. Fannie Farmer standardized the recipe, making it reproducible for home cooks across America.

recipes.title: New England Fish Chowder
recipes.description: Creamy, chunky fish chowder that defines New England cooking.
instructions: Render salt pork in a large pot until crispy. Remove cracklings and set aside.
Add onions to fat and cook until softened.
Add potatoes and water. Simmer until potatoes are tender, about 15 minutes.
Add fish. Simmer gently until fish is cooked through, about 10 minutes.
Add milk, cream, butter, salt, and pepper. Heat through but do not boil.
Let stand 30 minutes for flavors to meld. Reheat gently.
Serve topped with reserved cracklings and oyster crackers.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Chowder has been a New England staple since colonial times. Fannie Farmer's version emphasizes the cream and fish, creating the prototype for all fish chowders that followed.

recipes.title: Welsh Rarebit
recipes.description: A rich cheese sauce spooned over toast—simple, satisfying supper or lunch.
instructions: Melt butter in a double boiler or heavy saucepan over low heat.
Whisk in flour. Cook 1 minute.
Gradually add milk, whisking constantly.
Add cheese and stir until melted and smooth.
Beat egg yolk with a little of the hot cheese mixture to temper.
Return to pot. Add mustard, Worcestershire, cayenne, and salt.
Cook, stirring, until thickened. Do not boil.
Pour over toast and serve immediately.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Welsh Rarebit was a popular supper dish in the late 1800s. Fannie Farmer's recipe includes the trick of tempering the egg yolk to prevent curdling.

recipes.title: New England Clam Fritters
recipes.description: Light, crispy fritters studded with tender clams—a seaside favorite.

ingredients.name: clam juice
ingredients.notes: from canned clams, plus milk if needed

instructions: Whisk flour, baking powder, salt, and pepper.
Beat egg with clam juice and enough milk to equal 2/3 cup liquid.
Add wet ingredients to dry and stir until just combined.
Fold in chopped clams.
Heat oil to 375°F (190°C) in a deep pot.
Drop batter by tablespoons into hot oil.
Fry until golden brown, about 2-3 minutes, turning once.
Drain on paper towels. Serve immediately with lemon and tartar sauce.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Clam fritters were a popular way to stretch precious shellfish. Fannie Farmer's batter creates a light, crispy coating that lets the clam flavor shine through.

recipes.title: Codfish Balls
recipes.description: Crispy outside, fluffy inside—the classic New England breakfast.
instructions: Soak salt cod in cold water 24-48 hours, changing water several times.
Drain cod and place in a pot with potatoes. Cover with fresh water.
Bring to a boil and cook until potatoes are tender, about 20 minutes.
Drain well. Mash together with butter, egg, and pepper.
Shape into balls or patties.
Heat oil to 375°F (190°C).
Fry in batches until golden brown, about 3 minutes.
Drain on paper towels. Serve hot.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Salt cod was a New England staple before refrigeration. These crispy balls, served with baked beans and brown bread, were the traditional Saturday night supper.

recipes.title: Creamed Oysters on Toast
recipes.description: Delicate oysters in a rich cream sauce—an elegant supper from the Gilded Age.
instructions: Drain oysters, reserving liquor. Add milk to liquor to make 1 cup.
Melt butter in a saucepan. Whisk in flour and cook 1 minute.
Gradually whisk in oyster liquor mixture and cream.
Cook until thickened, about 3-4 minutes.
Add oysters, salt, white pepper, and cayenne.
Cook gently just until oyster edges curl, about 2-3 minutes. Do not overcook.
Spoon over toast points. Garnish with parsley.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: In the late 1800s, oysters were abundant and inexpensive. This elegant preparation transformed them into refined supper fare suitable for the finest tables.

recipes.title: Lobster Newburg
recipes.description: Succulent lobster in a rich, sherry-laced cream sauce—Gilded Age elegance.

ingredients.name: toast points or puff pastry shells

instructions: Melt butter in a heavy saucepan over medium heat.
Add lobster and cook gently for 2 minutes.
Add sherry and simmer 1 minute.
Whisk egg yolks with cream. Slowly add to the pan, stirring constantly.
Cook over low heat, stirring, until sauce thickens enough to coat a spoon. Do not boil.
Season with salt and cayenne.
Serve immediately over toast points or in puff pastry shells.
recipes.source: Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Fannie Farmer, 1896
recipes.story: Created at Delmonico's restaurant in New York, Lobster Newburg became a Gilded Age favorite. Fannie Farmer's recipe made this elegant dish accessible to home cooks.
